questions.title: Coagulation pathway selectively affected by low-dose heparin
questions.question: Low concentrations of heparin selectively interfere with which of the following coagulation pathway(s)?

explanations.A: Correct. At low concentration, heparin (via antithrombin III) preferentially inhibits factor Xa relative to thrombin, which has a disproportionate effect on the intrinsic pathway's amplification through the tenase complex. At higher concentrations, heparin's thrombin inhibition becomes prominent as well, extending its effect to the common pathway. This dose-dependent selectivity is why aPTT (sensitive to the intrinsic and common pathways) is the standard heparin-monitoring test.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Heparin has little effect on the extrinsic pathway (tested by PT), which is why PT/INR is used to monitor warfarin, not heparin.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The common pathway is only prominently affected at higher heparin concentrations, not at low, selective doses.
explanations.D: Incorrect. At low concentration, heparin's selective effect is on the intrinsic pathway alone, not both intrinsic and common together.

questions.learning_objective: State that low-dose heparin selectively affects the intrinsic coagulation pathway, a dose-dependent selectivity distinct from higher-dose effects on the common pathway.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.160, marginal note 'Power Qs'

questions.title: Drug reducing the effect of oral anticoagulants
questions.question: The following drug reduces the effect of oral anticoagulants:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Broad-spectrum antibiotics reduce gut-flora vitamin K synthesis, which potentiates (not reduces) warfarin's effect.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Cimetidine inhibits hepatic metabolism of warfarin, which potentiates (not reduces) its effect.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Aspirin adds antiplatelet bleeding risk on top of warfarin rather than reducing its anticoagulant effect.
explanations.D: Correct. Estrogen-containing oral contraceptives increase hepatic synthesis of several vitamin-K-dependent clotting factors, which partially offsets warfarin's inhibition of that same synthesis. The net effect is a reduced anticoagulant response to a given warfarin dose in a patient also taking oral contraceptives, requiring closer INR monitoring and possible dose adjustment when the two are combined.

questions.learning_objective: Identify oral contraceptives as reducing warfarin's anticoagulant effect, distinct from drugs (antibiotics, cimetidine) that potentiate it.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.160, marginal note 'Power Qs'

questions.title: Lab test for monitoring heparin therapy
questions.question: Heparin therapy is monitored by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate reflects inflammation, not coagulation status, and does not monitor heparin.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Alpha-2 antiplasmin level is not the standard heparin monitoring test.
explanations.C: Correct. Because heparin's major anticoagulant action works through the intrinsic and common coagulation pathways, activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) — which specifically tests those pathways — is the standard laboratory test used to monitor and titrate unfractionated heparin therapy, with a target typically 1.5-2.5 times the control value. This contrasts with warfarin, which is monitored using PT/INR, reflecting each drug's different site of action in the coagulation cascade.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Prothrombin time (PT/INR) monitors warfarin, not heparin.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Plasma fibrinogen concentration is not the standard heparin monitoring test.

questions.learning_objective: Identify activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) as the standard monitoring test for unfractionated heparin therapy.

questions.title: Major adverse effect of heparin
questions.question: The major adverse effect of heparin is:

explanations.A: Correct. As a directly-acting, rapidly-onset anticoagulant, heparin's dose-limiting and most clinically important adverse effect is bleeding, ranging from minor bruising and injection-site haematoma to major internal or intracranial haemorrhage. This is why heparin dosing is individualised and monitored by aPTT, and why a specific reversal agent (protamine sulfate) exists for rapid correction when bleeding occurs or urgent reversal is needed.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Heparin does not cross the placenta (unlike warfarin), so this is not an adverse effect at all, let alone the major one.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Hepatic transaminase elevation is not heparin's major or defining adverse effect.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Allergic reactions can occur with heparin but are not its major, most clinically significant adverse effect — bleeding is.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Heparin can rarely cause hypoaldosteronism with prolonged use, but this is not its major adverse effect.

questions.learning_objective: Identify bleeding as the major, dose-limiting adverse effect of heparin therapy.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.160

questions.title: Antagonist for heparin overdose
questions.question: Which of the following can be used to antagonize the action of heparin in case of heparin overdose?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Heparan/heparin sulfate is structurally related to heparin itself, not an antagonist.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Dextran sulfate is not heparin's reversal agent.
explanations.C: Correct. Heparin acts in vivo and in vitro with rapid onset, short duration, and injection route, and has protamine sulfate as its specific antidote. Protamine, a strongly basic protein, binds and neutralises heparin's strongly acidic charge, forming an inactive complex, giving rapid reversal of heparin's anticoagulant effect in overdose or before urgent procedures.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Ancrod is a defibrinogenating snake-venom-derived agent, not a heparin antagonist.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Vitamin K reverses warfarin, not heparin, since heparin's action is independent of vitamin K.

questions.learning_objective: Identify protamine sulfate as the specific antidote that reverses heparin's anticoagulant effect.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.161

questions.title: Heparin adverse effects EXCEPT
questions.question: Adverse effects of heparin include all of the following EXCEPT:

explanations.A: This is a recognised heparin adverse effect, not the exception. Hemorrhage/bleeding is heparin's major adverse effect.
explanations.B: Correct — this is the exception (NOT a heparin adverse effect), and therefore the answer. Heparin is a large, highly charged molecule that does not cross the placenta, so it does not reach the fetal circulation and is not associated with fetal malformations. Warfarin, by contrast, is small and lipophilic, crosses the placenta readily, and is teratogenic (warfarin embryopathy), which is why heparin (or LMWH) replaces warfarin whenever anticoagulation is needed in pregnancy.
explanations.C: This is a recognised heparin adverse effect, not the exception. Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia is a well-known immune complication of heparin therapy.
explanations.D: This is a recognised heparin adverse effect, not the exception. Alopecia can occur with prolonged heparin use.
explanations.E: This is a recognised heparin adverse effect, not the exception. Osteoporosis can occur with prolonged heparin use, from its effect on osteoblast/osteoclast activity.

questions.learning_objective: Identify fetal malformations as NOT a heparin adverse effect (since heparin does not cross the placenta), unlike warfarin.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.161

questions.title: Effect of sudden warfarin withdrawal
questions.question: Sudden withdrawal of warfarin leads to which of the following?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Alopecia is associated with prolonged heparin use, not warfarin withdrawal.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Hemorrhage would be expected from excess, not withdrawal, of warfarin's anticoagulant effect.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Osteoporosis is associated with prolonged heparin, not warfarin withdrawal.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Tachycardia is not the recognised effect of sudden warfarin withdrawal.
explanations.E: Correct. Warfarin inhibits synthesis of both procoagulant vitamin-K-dependent factors (II, VII, IX, X) and the anticoagulant proteins C and S, which are also vitamin-K-dependent. Because protein C has a shorter half-life than the procoagulant factors, abrupt warfarin withdrawal can transiently favour a procoagulant state, increasing thrombosis risk rather than simply returning to baseline coagulation. This is why warfarin is stopped with attention to timing rather than abruptly.

questions.learning_objective: State that sudden warfarin withdrawal can cause rebound thrombosis, from unbalanced loss of procoagulant vs anticoagulant vitamin-K-dependent factor suppression.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.161

questions.title: Reversal of excessive warfarin bleeding
questions.question: Excessive anticoagulant effect and bleeding from warfarin can be reversed by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) has no role in reversing warfarin.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Vitamin B12 has no role in reversing warfarin.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Vitamin C has no role in reversing warfarin.
explanations.D: Correct. Warfarin (dicumarol-class) acts only in vivo, with slow onset, long duration, oral route, and vitamin K as its antidote. Because warfarin blocks the vitamin-K-dependent gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX and X, giving vitamin K1 restores the substrate needed for hepatic synthesis of active clotting factors, reversing excessive anticoagulation and bleeding. This is the specific, mechanism-matched reversal for warfarin, distinct from protamine, which reverses heparin instead.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Protamine sulfate reverses heparin, not warfarin.

questions.learning_objective: Identify vitamin K1 as the specific reversal agent for excessive warfarin anticoagulation and bleeding.

questions.title: Route of heparin administration
questions.question: Which of the following is the route of heparin administration?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Heparin is not administered by inhalation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Intramuscular injection is avoided for heparin because it risks haematoma formation at the injection site in an anticoagulated patient.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Heparin cannot be given orally — it is a large, charged molecule that is not absorbed through the gut, which is exactly why warfarin (small, lipophilic, orally bioavailable) is used for long-term outpatient anticoagulation instead.
explanations.D: Correct. Heparin acts in vivo and in vitro with rapid onset, short duration, and injection route (IV or subcutaneous), with protamine sulfate as its specific antidote. Subcutaneous injection is the standard route for prophylactic dosing, while continuous IV infusion is used for full therapeutic anticoagulation.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Heparin is not given sublingually.

questions.learning_objective: Identify subcutaneous (or IV) injection as heparin's route of administration, since it is not orally bioavailable.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.162

questions.title: Injectable substitute for heparin in severe thrombocytopenia
questions.question: If a patient developed severe thrombocytopenia, an appropriate injectable substitute to heparin is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Enoxaparin, a low-molecular-weight heparin, still cross-reacts immunologically with heparin-PF4 antibodies in most heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) patients and is not considered a safe substitute.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Dicumarol is an oral vitamin-K antagonist, not an injectable heparin substitute for this setting.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Dalteparin is also an LMWH and, like enoxaparin, still cross-reacts in most HIT patients.
explanations.D: Correct. Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia is an immune reaction against heparin-platelet factor 4 complexes that paradoxically causes both thrombocytopenia and a high risk of thrombosis, so simply stopping heparin is not enough. Hirudin, a direct thrombin inhibitor, works independently of antithrombin and does not share heparin's antigenic complex, making it an appropriate injectable substitute in this setting.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Phenindione is an oral vitamin-K antagonist, not an injectable heparin substitute.

questions.learning_objective: Identify hirudin (a direct thrombin inhibitor) as an appropriate injectable substitute for heparin in heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, distinguishing it from LMWH, which still cross-reacts.

questions.title: How LMWH differs from unfractionated heparin
questions.question: Low molecular weight heparins differ from unfractionated heparin in which of the following?

options.C: They have a shorter duration of action

explanations.A: Correct. Unfractionated heparin's longer chains can bind both antithrombin and thrombin simultaneously, potentiating antithrombin's inhibition of thrombin as well as factor Xa. Low-molecular-weight heparins, being shorter chains (e.g. enoxaparin), are usually too short to bridge antithrombin to thrombin but retain the ability to potentiate antithrombin's inhibition of factor Xa, giving them a selectively anti-Xa profile. This more predictable dosing profile is why LMWHs are widely used without requiring routine aPTT monitoring, unlike unfractionated heparin.
explanations.B: Incorrect. LMWH's anti-Xa-predominant effect does not prolong clotting time (a thrombin-dependent test) the way unfractionated heparin does — this is part of why aPTT does not reliably reflect LMWH dosing.
explanations.C: Incorrect. LMWH actually has a longer, not shorter, duration of action and half-life than unfractionated heparin, allowing once- or twice-daily dosing.
explanations.D: Incorrect. LMWH is typically given subcutaneously, not IV only.
explanations.E: Incorrect. LMWH requires less frequent (often no routine) monitoring, the opposite of unfractionated heparin, which needs individualised aPTT titration.

questions.learning_objective: State that LMWH selectively inhibits factor Xa (chains too short to bridge antithrombin to thrombin), unlike unfractionated heparin's balanced anti-Xa/anti-thrombin action.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.162

questions.title: Contraindication of heparin
questions.question: Which of the following is a contraindication of heparin?

explanations.A: Incorrect. COVID-19 pneumonia is, if anything, associated with increased thrombosis risk, making heparin prophylaxis appropriate, not contraindicated.
explanations.B: Correct. Because bleeding is heparin's major adverse effect, active or recent significant bleeding — such as a bleeding peptic ulcer — is a clear contraindication, since anticoagulation would worsen an already-bleeding lesion. Conditions like pulmonary embolism or post-surgical thrombosis risk, by contrast, are indications for heparin, because they carry thrombosis risk that heparin's benefit is meant to address.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Pulmonary embolism is a treatment indication for heparin, not a contraindication.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Hip replacement surgery is a classic indication for thromboprophylaxis with heparin (or LMWH), not a contraindication.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Pregnancy is not a contraindication to heparin; heparin does not cross the placenta and is the anticoagulant of choice in pregnancy.

questions.learning_objective: Identify active/recent significant bleeding (e.g. bleeding peptic ulcer) as a heparin contraindication, distinguishing it from thrombosis-risk conditions that are indications instead.

questions.title: Primary mechanism by which heparin prevents coagulation
questions.question: Which of the following is the primary mechanism by which heparin prevents coagulation of blood?

options.A: Direct inhibition of prothrombin to thrombin conversion
options.B: Facilitation of antithrombin III mediated inhibition of factor Xa and thrombin
options.C: Activation of antithrombin III to inhibit factors IX and XI
options.D: Inhibition of factors XIIa and XIIIa
options.E: Inhibition of the synthesis of prothrombin

explanations.A: Incorrect. Heparin does not directly inhibit the prothrombin-to-thrombin conversion enzymatically; it works through antithrombin III.
explanations.B: Correct. Heparin facilitates antithrombin III's inhibition of activated clotting factors, most importantly factor IXa, Xa, XIa and XIIa, and thrombin (IIa) — the option here summarising this as facilitation of antithrombin-mediated inhibition of factor Xa and thrombin. Heparin itself has no direct enzymatic anticoagulant action; it works entirely by massively accelerating antithrombin's own natural inhibitory activity against these activated factors.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Heparin's target factors for antithrombin-mediated inhibition are primarily Xa and thrombin (IIa), not specifically 'IX and XI' as framed here.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Heparin's mechanism is not framed as direct inhibition of XIIa and XIIIa; its action is via antithrombin potentiation.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Heparin does not inhibit prothrombin synthesis (that is warfarin's mechanism); it inhibits already-activated clotting factors via antithrombin.

questions.learning_objective: State that heparin's primary mechanism is facilitating antithrombin III's inhibition of activated clotting factors (factor Xa and thrombin chief among them), not any direct enzymatic action.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.163
field_notes.reuse: Reuses live concept CON-HEM-FF26A3D7EE6DB7 ('Heparin facilitates antithrombin III inhibition of IXa, Xa, XIa, and XIIa') directly — live target, no overlay needed.

questions.title: Proposed mechanism of action of warfarin
questions.question: Warfarin is an anticoagulant. Its proposed mechanism of action is that it:

options.E: Inhibits synthesis of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors

explanations.A: Incorrect. Warfarin does not inhibit platelet production; that is not its mechanism.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Blocking prostaglandin synthesis describes aspirin's antiplatelet mechanism, not warfarin's.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Warfarin does not block vitamin K absorption in the gut; it acts intracellularly in the liver on vitamin K recycling.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Warfarin does not bind fibrinogen directly.
explanations.E: Correct. Coumarins (warfarin) competitively inhibit vitamin K epoxide reductase, blocking the recycling of vitamin K needed for hepatic gamma-carboxylation and formation of prothrombin and factors VII, IX and X. Unlike heparin, which acts on already-formed, circulating clotting factors, warfarin acts by suppressing new synthesis of these factors in the liver, which is also why its onset is slow (limited by the clearance of pre-existing factors) and why it needs bridging with heparin at initiation.

questions.learning_objective: State that warfarin's mechanism is inhibiting hepatic synthesis of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors, distinct from heparin's action on already-formed factors.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.163

questions.title: Primary advantage of enoxaparin over heparin
questions.question: The primary advantage of enoxaparin over heparin is that it:

options.B: More effectively inhibits the synthesis of clotting factors

explanations.A: Correct (as printed). This department bank's printed answer credits enoxaparin with being less likely to cause bleeding than unfractionated heparin. The more standard pharmacology teaching frames LMWH's advantages as more predictable, weight-based dosing, a longer half-life allowing once- or twice-daily dosing without routine monitoring, and a lower risk of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia and osteoporosis — with bleeding risk itself considered broadly comparable in most comparative studies. The printed key is followed here as authored, with this discrepancy flagged.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Neither LMWH nor unfractionated heparin inhibits clotting factor synthesis; that is warfarin's mechanism, not heparin-family drugs'.
explanations.C: Incorrect. LMWH does not have a more rapid onset than unfractionated heparin; both act quickly, but this is not the cited advantage.
explanations.D: Incorrect. LMWH has a lower, but not zero, risk of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia — 'does not cause' overstates the advantage.
explanations.E: Incorrect. LMWH has a longer, not shorter, half-life than unfractionated heparin, which is part of why it can be dosed once or twice daily.

questions.learning_objective: Reproduce this bank's printed framing of enoxaparin's advantage over heparin (lower bleeding likelihood), while recognising the more standard textbook advantages (predictable dosing, lower HIT/osteoporosis risk).

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.163
